Toss perfection aside and embrace the quirks

As a kid, I used to tape faces onto inanimate objects and instantly fall in love. The light in my bedroom was just an appliance, until I stuck on googly eyes, a crooked nose and a smile. Overnight, metal and glass became “Lampy,” my trusted nighttime companion.

That instinct to project humanity everywhere reveals something fundamental about how we form attachments. We are hardwired to look for faces, seek kinship and bond through empathy.

For decades, consumer brands have leaned into that exact psychological shortcut. A well-crafted mascot is often among a brand’s highest-value assets, translating abstract themes into immediate emotional connections. Nowhere has this been more potent, or nostalgic, than in the food aisle. I grew up alongside Cap’n Crunch, Tony the Tiger, and Ronald McDonald. Today, we’re witnessing a major mascot resurgence. Cornelius Rooster is proudly reclaiming the center stage of Kellogg’s corn flakes. The Pillsbury Doughboy is back with his signature chuckle. Chester Cheetah continues to bring disruptive, chaotic energy to Cheetos.

But with emotional resonance comes real responsibility. In an era where families demand ingredient transparency and ethical marketing, the guardrails around how and why we design characters for food brands matter more than ever. Here is what designers and brand leaders need to keep in mind when giving life to a brand.

Beyond the Logo: Build a Living Personality System Designing a character today goes far beyond drawing a charming visual for packaging or a 30-second spot. You are architecting a complete personality system. The character must look, speak, emote and move seamlessly across 2D packaging, 3D gaming spaces, social motion and physical merchandise, all while remaining unmistakably cohesive.

You also face an essential strategic question: Does the character exist merely to endorse the food or is it bigger than the product? Tony the Tiger doesn’t merely love breakfast cereal. He has evolved into a proponent for youth sports and the importance of play. 

Personality Over Perfection: Embrace the Quirks With countless illustrated figures vying for attention, anodyne perfection is fatal—and a surefire way to trigger accusations of AI usage. The characters that endure aren’t pristine corporate archetypes; rather, they carry genuine edge, charm and human vulnerability. Even classic tropes, like an energetic bunny or a swashbuckling adventurer, only work when anchored by an authentic attitude. In our work with Pirate’s Booty, the mandate was to liberate their fearless mascot, unlocking a world of delicious mischief that gave him enough dimension to delight kids and amuse parents simultaneously.

Ethical Guardrails: Design for Responsibility When a brand character speaks directly to children, you have to be deliberate about how, where and whether it engages. Ethical design isn’t just about adhering to evolving legal standards; it’s about brand stewardship. Defining explicit boundaries prevents a character from crossing the line from playful engagement into manipulative marketing. A mascot needs clear rules of engagement to remain both beloved and responsible.

Intentional Craft: Don’t Let Generative AI Dilute the Core Generative AI makes it tempting to spin up infinite character variations in seconds, but shortcuts erode equity. The more rigorously you document your character’s proportions, silhouette rules, vocal tone and attitudes while they are being created, the more resilient they become against generic, off-brand drift.

Highlighting the deliberate human craft behind a character, the intentional choices behind an expressive eyebrow or an imperfect gait, protects its narrative integrity at a time when AI output risks commoditizing visual charm.

Related: Don’t Rush to Judge Liberty Biberty. The Data Says Wait

Drew Stocker is a creative director at Pearlfisher.
